catalog_citation: Quakenbush, J. Stephen, Gail R. Hendrickson & Josenita L. Edep. 2010. A Brief Overview of Agutaynen Grammar. Manila: SIL Philippines (electronic publication, ISBN 978-971-18-0435-0). Secondary check: Quakenbush, J. Stephen. 1991. Agutaynen Glottal Stop. Work …
catalog_locator: Appendix 1 'Some Agutaynen sound patterns', subsection 'Stress', p. 40 (long-vowel orthography note: section 2, p. 3; syllable types CV.V / CV.VC p. 39)
catalog_quote: Stress falls predictably on the penultimate syllable of words in isolated elicitation. Although it has not been formally investigated, it seems that placement of stress occurs more on a sentence or phrase level rather than on the word level. Stress on individual words loses importance in an extended utterance.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held 2010 sketch at Appendix 1 'Stress', p. 40, exactly as the locator says; the supporting syllable-type and macron notes (pp. 39, 3) are also there. (2) Deciding source: a 2010 SIL grammar sketch by the language's principal fieldworkers; the stress statement is brief and self-declared 'not formally investigated', with a caveat that stress may be phrase-level. Held secondary Quakenbush 1991 (fn. 9: stress 'plays a very minimal role'; no stress/length in the phoneme table) and newly downloaded Himes 2006 (p. 2: Proto-Kalamian 'seems to have lost stress as a phonemic feature') both point the same way: non-contrastive stress, consistent with fixed penultimate in citation forms. The 2014 LSP dictionary's grammar sketch is the same text (Webonary phonology page reproduces it verbatim), so it would not upgrade the record. Glottolog's rem

sources.citation: Himes, Ronald S. 2006. The Kalamian microgroup of Philippine languages. Paper presented at the Tenth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics (10-ICAL), Puerto Princesa, Palawan, 17-20 January 2006. 23 pp. (SIL Philippines ICAL papers site, Internet Archive copy).
sources.quote: 'The four PPh vowels are *i, *e (schwa), *u and *a. Stress was also phonemic in PPh. Proto-Kalamian (PKlm) seems to have lost stress as a phonemic feature.' (Kalamian = Agutaynen + Kalamian Tagbanwa dialects; Agutaynen data from Himes's own fieldwork 1964, 2001, 2003.)
sources.note: Independent comparative statement that Proto-Kalamian lost phonemic stress, supporting non-contrastive (predictable) stress in Agutaynen; could be added as a secondary source on the record.

sources.citation: Agutaynen Dictionary, online edition (Linguistic Society of the Philippines / SIL, Webonary, published 2018-03-29; from Caabay, Melvin, Hendrickson, Quakenbush & Edep 2014, Agutaynen-English Dictionary). 'Phonology' page.
sources.quote: No stress statement; page reproduces section 2 of the 2010 sketch verbatim (20 phonemes, 4 vowels; macron = two identical vowels, e.g. maboat 'can be done' vs māboat 'long', tolok 'torch' vs tolōk 'crow of a rooster'). Confirms the 2014 dictionary's sketch is the same text as the 2010 deciding source. A browse page (letter t) shows an occasional acute on a headword variant ('ta rá', var. of maytara 'Let's go!'), i.e. stress marks appear only exceptionally.
sources.locator: Language > Phonology page ('2. The sounds and spelling of Agutaynen')

tone.summary: No tone content. Word prosody as stated: stress penultimate in citation forms, described as phrase/sentence-level rather than word-level; orthographic long vowels = two identical vowels; acute accent marks stress on c. 135 (mostly oxytone) headwords.
